primary_sources: Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917 (public domain).
stimulus.text:
President Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917 (verbatim excerpts):

"... I advise that the Congress declare the recent course of the Imperial German Government to be in fact nothing less than war against the Government and people of the United States; that it formally accept the status of belligerent which has thus been thrust upon it..."

. . .

"But the right is more precious than peace, and we shall fight for the things which we have always carried nearest our hearts — for democracy, for the right of those who submit to authority to have a voice in their own governments, for the rights and liberties of small nations, for a universal dominion of right by such a concert of free peoples as shall bring peace and safety to all nations and make the world itself at last free."

. . .

"The world must be made safe for democracy. Its peace must be planted upon the tested foundations of political liberty. We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion. We seek no indemnities for ourselves, no material compensation for the sacrifices we shall freely make."

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Woodrow Wilson, War Message to Congress, April 2, 1917
stem: Wilson's claim that "the right is more precious than peace" best shows that he

options.text: believed the United States should have entered the war in 1914
options.misconception: Wilson waited until 1917 and ran in 1916 on keeping the country out of war. The line explains why he changed, not that he wanted war in 1914.

options.text: thought peace with Germany was still possible in April 1917
options.misconception: Wilson is asking Congress to declare war, so he is not saying peace is still possible. The line says the right matters more than keeping the peace.

options.text: wanted Congress to reject the declaration of war
options.misconception: Wilson is urging Congress to accept war, not reject it. The passage asks Congress to declare the state of war that already exists.

options.text: ranked defending democratic rights above staying out of the war

rationales.A: Wilson waited until 1917 and ran in 1916 on keeping the country out of war. The line explains why he changed, not that he wanted war in 1914.
rationales.B: Wilson is asking Congress to declare war, so he is not saying peace is still possible. The line says the right matters more than keeping the peace.
rationales.C: Wilson is urging Congress to accept war, not reject it. The passage asks Congress to declare the state of war that already exists.
rationales.D: Wilson says the right is worth more than peace itself, then lists the rights he means: democracy, a voice in government, and the rights of small nations. He is ranking those rights above staying out of the war.
rationales.general:
1. Find the ranking in the sentence. Wilson puts the right above peace.
2. Find what the right means here. The sentence goes on to name democracy, a voice in government, and the rights of small nations.
3. Background from the books: Wilson had kept the country neutral for nearly three years, so this sentence explains a change of mind, not a long-held wish for war.
Remember: a sentence that ranks one value above another tells you what the speaker is willing to give up.
